extracted.intended_audience: educated lay readers and natural philosophers (skeptics/atheists)
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-science / natural-theology exposition of the physical properties of light (velocity, rectilinear propagation, divergence, refraction, heating power) used to argue for design and divine governance. The text mixes experimental references, calculations, and thought experiments to persuade educated non-specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence for a finite speed of light
rubrics_metrics.description: Light requires some measurable time to pass from the Sun to the Earth (the author cites values around seven to ten minutes) rather than being instantaneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept claims of finite light-speed only when supported by experiments and astronomical observations: Romer's ten years of observations on Jupiter's satellites (timing of eclipses), Newton's and Huygens' analyses, and later confirmations. The text references Newton's Principia/Opticks and Huygens' Treatise of Light as primary proofs. Use these experimental/observational records rather than mere hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light propagates in straight (rectilinear) lines
rubrics_metrics.description: One property of light is that it moves in right lines; this rectilinear motion accounts for the formation of shadows and the rules of perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is supported by experiment and geometrical reasoning (cones of shadow from points on the Sun). Use ray diagrams (points A, B to P forming cones/pyramids of shadow) to demonstrate how straight-line propagation yields regions of darkness; if light moved in arbitrary curves there would be no well-defined shadows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence of rays and inverse-square diminution
rubrics_metrics.description: Rays from a point in the Sun diverge as they travel, so the same bundle of rays occupies progressively larger areas; therefore intensity/heat decreases as (roughly) the square of the distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geometric proportions to compute relative heating: compare the area of small and large circles cut by rays at different distances (example: when SB is twice Sb the heat at the nearer circle is four times that at the farther). Burning-glass experiments and numerical examples (squares of distances like 100^2 vs 5^2) illustrate the rule. Apply this when estimating thermal effects at different distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental demonstration that light carries fire/heat and can exert mechanical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Light is either fire itself or carries a substantial quantity of fire; concentrated rays (e.g., in a burning-glass focus) can melt metals, ignite wood, and even mechanically move light-weight objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on documented experiments (Homberg's burning-glass experiments, observations in the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Sciences) showing that materials like amianthus or a watch spring placed in the focus are driven/moved or ignited. Use such experimental demonstrations as evidence for the combustive and mechanical powers of light rather than mere analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refraction as necessary for distinct vision and moderation of daylight
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides rectilinear and divergent propagation, refraction is a separate law by which rays are bent and gathered so that distinct images form and so that dawn/dusk transition (twilight) is gradual rather than instantaneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain distinct vision by showing that rays from different points of an object are inflected (refracted) and collected into particular image points; invoke figures (object AB, rays filling space AST, gathering at SOT producing distinct view at ST). Also argue that refraction spreads the sunrise/sunset over time, protecting eyes from abrupt transitions. Treat refraction as a structural law required to make vision useful to organisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refraction obeys a regular relation between incident and refracted angles
rubrics_metrics.description: When a ray meets an interface (e.g., water surface) at a point O it does not continue straight but makes an angle (is refracted) according to a geometrical relation; refracted rays proceed along a definite line (the refracted ray).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support claims by experiment: trace rays SO to interface FG and measure angles BOP and bOp; use geometric construction (center O and circles) to demonstrate breaking and new direction. Use these geometric/experimental prescriptions when describing or calculating refraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence of rays as a protective mechanism for the Earth
rubrics_metrics.description: The continual scattering/divergence of solar rays as they travel is what chiefly prevents the Earth from being consumed by the Sun's fire; were the rays collected, they would produce destructive heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thought experiments: imagine rays descending compact as near the Sun (or becoming parallel/collected) to show that focus would melt or consume Earthly materials. Emphasize divergence (not merely distance) as the key protective factor; refer to burning-glass analogies to quantify danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative, multiple-method estimates to convey astronomical magnitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: To grasp solar distances, speed-of-light effects, or total light quantity, present several numeric computations (e.g., sun-earth distance in earth diameters/ Dutch leagues/ French fathoms; time for a horse/ship or cannon-ball to reach the Sun; seconds/minutes for light travel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide different calculation methods and units (diameters, leagues, fathoms), show intermediate arithmetic (products, divisions), and compare results (e.g., 12000 diameters × Earth semidiameter → league/fathom numbers; dividing by 50 miles/day → years). Use these concrete numbers and comparative analogies to counter anthropocentric underestimation of cosmic scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of experimental corroboration over speculative hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about light (velocity, rectilinear motion, refractive laws, combustive properties) should be established by experiment and observed astronomical phenomena rather than mere speculative analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize references to experiments and authoritative observers: Romer, Newton, Huygens, Whiston, the Royal Academy reports. Where an idea might seem incredible, appeal to experimental confirmations (eclipses timing, burning-glass effects) and mathematical demonstration to render it incontestable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling the mechanical effects of light via comparison to projectiles
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate force exerted by an aggregate of light, compare its velocity and occupied distance-per-time to that of known projectiles, using the product of weight × distance moved in the same time as proportional to force (from mechanics of percussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the rule of three: equate (weight × distance) for a known cannon shot and solve for the equivalent weight of light that would yield the same effect at its higher velocity. The text gives a worked example yielding a minute weight of light equivalent to a 12-pound shot, and translates into grains; use these mechanics-based scaling calculations with caution (historic mechanical model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergency yields two practical benefits: safety and all-around illumination
rubrics_metrics.description: From the divergence of rays follow (1) protection of the Earth from conflagration and (2) the fact that bodies are illuminated from all sides (rays scatter to render small points visible around).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining the usefulness of divergence, cite both consequences: safety (preventing concentrated burning) and function (point P becoming visible from surrounding directions due to separation of rays). Use ray diagrams (candle K, rays KP) as illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refraction and twilight as designed solutions to sensory and environmental problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Refraction both allows distinct vision (by gathering rays) and prevents abrupt changes of illumination at sunrise/sunset (twilight), solving practical problems that would otherwise harm vision or life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame refraction as an explanatory law that addresses specific functional problems; use the example of sudden transition from full daylight to pitch-dark night as the problem, and show how refracted rays and atmospheric effects produce gradual light transitions. This is used rhetorically to support teleological conclusions, so when adopting this criterion separate physical explanation from theological inference.
